paragraphs: On a summer afternoon, walking from a city park into a busy street feels like opening an oven door. This is not just an impression. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island.

The causes are well understood. Asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so cities cool down far less than rural areas. Tall buildings trap warm air and block the wind, while cars, air conditioners and industry add extra heat. Meanwhile, there are fewer trees and less vegetation, which in the countryside cool the air by providing shade and releasing water.

As heatwaves become more frequent and intense with climate change, the consequences are serious. Extreme heat is linked to thousands of deaths every year, mostly among elderly people, young children and those with health problems. The effects are not distributed equally either: poorer neighbourhoods often have fewer trees and parks than wealthier ones, and their residents are less likely to have air conditioning.

Cities around the world are looking for solutions. Medellín, in Colombia, has turned roads and streams into "green corridors" full of plants and trees, which have reportedly lowered temperatures in the surrounding streets by around two degrees. Paris has been transforming school playgrounds, replacing asphalt with trees and surfaces that absorb water, so that they can serve as cool spaces for neighbours during heatwaves. Other cities paint roofs white to reflect sunlight or require new buildings to include green roofs.
Air conditioning provides immediate relief, but it is not a perfect answer. It consumes large amounts of energy and pumps hot air into the street, which makes the problem worse outside.

Experts agree that there is no single solution. Planting trees, however, comes close: a mature tree can cool its surroundings, absorb rainwater, clean the air and make streets more pleasant to walk along. The challenge is that trees take decades to grow, so the best time to plant them, as an old saying goes, was twenty years ago.
